DBCnRoOcsQQ.title: All Done in Baby Sign Language, ASL

en.title: Week 4
en.oneLiner: She’s in a calmer, more independent stretch. This week: step practice twice a day, echo-and-point for words, and start a goodbye routine before the next wave (walking + daycare) arrives.
now: 🪜 Stairs up, and now steps down smoothly
🛒 Good with the push walker · pushes a ride-on
🤲 Asks to walk holding both your hands
🧍 Stands alone a few seconds (without noticing)
🗣️ baba · mama · yeye · baibai, with meaning
🖊️ Talking pen: points at books to play sounds
😌 Calmer · explores on her own · warms up to people faster

bigThree.title: Do “couch to Mama” steps, twice a day
lines: When: after her morning nap and before the afternoon playground, barefoot, on a clear floor. Stop while she’s still having fun.

How: she sits on your lap one small step from the couch, with a toy on the seat. Stand her up and let her step to it. Next time, sit a little farther away. Then switch: she starts at the couch and steps to you.
Help less each day: hold her hips, then her forearms (no higher than her shoulders), then just a finger. Give her a big ball to carry so her hands are busy.
Say: “Come to Mama!” (open arms, wait). If she steps: “You walked to me!” If she sits down: “Plop! Up again?” No big cheers or clapping, which can startle her down.
If she crawls instead, that’s fine. Try again later.

bigThree.title: Echo, point, name: 3 times a day
lines: When: breakfast, pen-book time, and the walk to the playground.
How 1, echo and add: she says “baba” → you say “Baba! Baba’s at work.” Repeat her word and add a little.
How 2, follow her point: look where she points, then name it: “Bird! A bird is flying.” Then point to something yourself and wait for her to look.
How 3, pen-book turns: she presses, you say the word (“Cat! Meow.”), then it’s her turn again.
Pause 3–5 seconds before a word she knows (“Bai…”). If she doesn’t say it, just say it yourself and move on.
Don’t say: “Say mama! Say it again!” She says words when she needs them, not on request.

bigThree.title: Start a goodbye routine before the next wave
lines: When: 3 times this week, while she’s calm and fed, with a grandparent or another familiar adult. Try 5 minutes, then 10, then 20.
How: same steps every time. Get down to her level, give a hug, say the goodbye line, wave, and leave even if she cries. Come back warm and unhurried.
Say leaving: “Mama’s going out. Grandma stays with you. Mama comes back.” → “Bye bye!”
Say returning: “Mama’s back! I said I’d come back.” Then sit with her for a few minutes.
Don’t: sneak out while she’s busy. Use this exact routine on the daycare first day.

cards.title: Where she is now: body
lines: Her legs are strong enough. What’s still growing is balance: letting go and catching herself.
Standing alone without noticing is the usual step right before first steps on her own.
Walking with both your hands, push walker, slides, stairs: all real balance practice. Barefoot helps her feet feel the floor.
Her hands are getting precise too: small food pieces, the pen tip on a picture.
Where it’s heading: 1–3 wobbly steps toward you, then walking with arms up and many falls. Anywhere from now to ~18 months is normal.

cards.title: Where she is now: brain and words
lines: She understands many more words than she says: names, “bye,” “no,” “where’s Baba?”
baba, mama, yeye, baibai used for the right person or moment = real first words. Two languages count together.
Saying a word on request is a separate, harder skill. It usually comes later. Words now pop out when she wants something or something happens.
Pointing with the pen = she knows a picture stands for a thing, and that pressing makes a sound (cause and effect).
Can’t yet: follow 2-step directions, remember rules (“no throwing”) from one meal to the next, or wait.

cards.title: Where she is now: feelings
lines: Last week’s fussy, clingy dip has passed. Now that she can get around and explore on her own, she is happier and calmer.
She plays alone longer, goes farther from you, and glances back to check in. That glance is how she refuels.
She warms up to new people faster. She may still watch from your lap first, and that’s fine.
Throwing food and watching your face is still experimenting (what happens? how does Mama react?), not naughtiness.

What comes next: babies move in cycles. A calm, capable stretch often comes before a new wave of clinginess when a big change arrives. For her, that’s walking (the world suddenly feels bigger) and daycare. Expect more protest at goodbyes, extra night waking, and wanting you close. It’s the next cycle starting, not going backwards.

cards.title: Do & don’t: first steps
lines: ✅ Do hold her at the hips or ribs, or her forearms at shoulder height or lower. Why: she uses her own balance, not your pull.
✅ Do put toys on the couch or give her a ball to carry with both hands. Why: busy hands let go of you without her noticing.
✅ Do stay barefoot indoors; soft, flexible shoes only outside. Why: toes grip and feet send balance signals.
🚫 Don’t walk her long distances with arms high over her head. Why: she tips forward on her toes and runs to catch up.
🚫 Don’t use a sit-in baby walker. Why: AAP: it causes injuries and doesn’t help walking.

refs.label: AAP/HealthyChildren: Baby walkers, a dangerous choice

cards.title: Do & don’t: words
cards.sub: Why she won’t say it again
lines: ✅ Do echo and add: she says “baba” → “Baba! Baba’s home!” Why: she hears her word back plus one more.
✅ Do pause 3–5 seconds before a known word (“Bye-…”), then say it yourself if she doesn’t. Why: a turn without pressure.
✅ Do keep both languages. Why: bilingual babies reach milestones on time when you count both.
🚫 Don’t “Say mama! Say it for Grandma!” Why: performing is hard and testing makes babies go quiet. Words come out when they’re useful to her, not on cue.
🚫 Don’t correct her sounds. Why: just say the word clearly back.

cards.title: Do & don’t: food flying
lines: Why: smashing = feeling textures. Throwing = cause and effect (it falls! Mama reacts!). Often it also means “I’m full.”
✅ Do serve 2–3 pieces at a time, add more when asked. Why: less to throw, easier to show “more.”
✅ Do say once, calmly: “Food stays on the table.” Show the “all done” sign. Why: she gets a way to say done.
✅ Do end the meal calmly if throwing continues. Why: it’s info, not a fight. Next meal is a fresh start.
🚫 Don’t laugh, scold loudly, or chase her with bites. Why: a big reaction is the best show in town, so she repeats it.
Play with throwing elsewhere: balls into a basket.

cards.title: Do & don’t: pointing and sharing
lines: When she points, looks back at you, then looks at a thing, she is sharing her mind with you. Big early language step.
✅ Do look where she points, name it, add a little: “Dog! A big dog!” Why: the word lands right when she’s interested.
✅ Do point yourself and wait for her to look. Make the pen book a two-person game: her press, your word.
🚫 Don’t leave the pen to “teach” her alone all the time. Why: babies learn words from people, not from sounds alone.

cards.title: Do & don’t: the next goodbye wave
lines: She’s calmer now and warms up faster. Enjoy it, and use this calm stretch to build the routine she’ll need next.
✅ Do let new people take their time. They talk to you first while she watches. Why: she reads your face to decide if someone is safe.
✅ Do practice short goodbyes now, while she’s calm. Why: each time you come back, her trust grows, and that carries her through the daycare wave.
✅ Do expect more clinginess when she starts walking or starts daycare. Why: a big new skill or change often brings a new round of needing you. It’s a new cycle, not going backwards.
🚫 Don’t sneak out. Why: she learns you can disappear without warning, and she clings harder.
Daycare first-day page has the full goodbye script and packing list.

cards.title: Do & don’t: teething
lines: ✅ Do rub her gums with a clean finger; offer a chilled (not frozen) teether. Why: pressure and cold soothe.
✅ Do brush twice a day with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste. Why: new teeth decay easily.
🚫 Don’t use numbing gels (benzocaine), teething tablets, or amber necklaces. Why: FDA and AAP warn of real risks.
Fever of 100.4°F / 38°C or more is not from teething. Ask the pediatrician about pain medicine doses.

refs.label: FDA: teething jewelry and gels warning

cards.title: What’s next: walking
lines: First she notices she is standing and stays up longer on purpose.
Then she stands up from a squat in the open, without holding anything.
Then 1–3 steps between couch and you, falling into your arms. Feet wide, arms up: that’s normal.
Then she walks more than she crawls, with lots of sitting falls. Falls on her bottom are how balance gets tuned.
Shoes come in when she walks outside a lot: light, flexible, wide toe.

cards.title: What’s next: words and understanding
lines: She’ll follow simple one-step requests with a gesture (“Give me the ball”).
Pointing to ask (“that one!”) and to show (“look!”) grows.
New words come slowly at first, often 1 every week or two, then faster after ~18 months.
Expect word-like sounds and half words (“ba” for ball). Count them if she uses them the same way each time.
By ~15 months, CDC expects 1–2 words besides mama/baba, counting both languages.

cards.title: What’s next: feelings, food, sleep
lines: Feelings: the calm stretch now usually gives way to a new wave around walking and daycare: more protest at goodbyes, wanting you close, night waking for a week or two. After that comes “I do it myself.” Hold limits calmly and comfort her; that’s the whole plan.
Food: family foods in small pieces, eating with fingers, then trying a spoon. Milk at one switch starts at 12 months.
Sleep: after 12 months, a small light blanket or soft toy can be added to the floor bed if you want. Most keep 2 naps until 13–18 months.
Daycare: a week or two of rough sleep or extra clinginess after starting is common and passes.

daily: Barefoot walking practice: hands-busy carry or toys on the couch
Hip or forearm support walks, not arms high
Stairs and slides with you below her
Follow 3 of her points and name what she sees
Pen-book time together: her press, your word
Small portions + “all done” sign at each meal
Gum rub or chilled teether when fussy
todos: Clear a flat “walking runway” at home (no rugs that slip)
Tell grandparents: no “say it!” testing, just echo her words
Make the goodbye ritual: same words, wave, kiss
2–3 practice separations with a familiar adult
Splat mat under the high chair
Set up the water table (always within arm’s reach)
Throw out any teething gels or amber necklaces

quiz.q: Walk her around the park holding both hands up high?
quiz.why: Short is fine for fun, but hands high tips her forward. Support at hips or forearms at shoulder height or lower.

quiz.q: She says “baba” → you say “Baba! Baba’s here!”
quiz.why: Echo and add: her word plus one more. This is how words grow.

quiz.q: “Say yeye for Yeye! Come on, say it!”
quiz.why: On-request words come later. Pressure makes her go quiet.

quiz.q: She throws peas. Say calmly “Food stays on the table” and offer the all-done sign?
quiz.why: Calm, short, and gives her a way to say she’s done.

quiz.q: Laugh hard the first time she throws food?
quiz.why: A big reaction is a great show, so she does it again.

quiz.q: Slip out while she plays so she doesn’t cry?
quiz.why: Sneaking out makes her clingier. Say bye, wave, leave, come back warmly.

quiz.q: Use a benzocaine numbing gel for teething?
quiz.why: FDA warns against it for babies. Use gum rubs and chilled teethers.

quiz.q: Look where she points and name it?
quiz.why: Joint attention: the word lands exactly when she is interested.

plays.name: Couch to Mama
plays.how: Lap → step to toys on the couch, then couch → your arms. Move a little farther each day. (from Wk 3 “One step to me”)

plays.name: Hands-busy standing
plays.how: Big light ball or two clappers to hold. Busy hands let go without noticing. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Wider stand-to-stand gap
plays.how: Two sturdy pieces of furniture, now a full step apart, so she has to let go and step across. (Wk 3, harder)

plays.name: Squat-to-pick-up, in the open
plays.how: Toy by her feet while she stands without holding on. Squat, grab, stand back up. (Wk 3, harder)

plays.name: One-hand walk
plays.how: Hold one hand at her shoulder height, toy in her other hand. Switch sides.

plays.name: Push-walker delivery
plays.how: A toy in the walker: “Take it to Baba!” Weigh it down if it rolls too fast. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Stairs down with a rail
plays.how: She already steps down smoothly. Now: one hand on the rail or wall, you one step below. (Wk 3, harder)

plays.name: Playground mission
plays.how: Pick ONE stretch per visit (a new climber, a bigger slide with you at the bottom). Stop while she’s happy. (Wk 1)

plays.name: Bring-it delivery, 2 steps
plays.how: “Pick up the ball and give it to Grandma.” Help with a gesture. (Wk 1, harder)

plays.name: Throw into the basket
plays.how: Balls into a laundry basket: “Throw! In!” The yes-place for throwing.

plays.name: Point-and-name walk
plays.how: Carry or walk her around: “Where’s the light?” When she points, look and name it. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Pen-book turns
plays.how: She presses, you say the word and add one, then it’s her turn. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Echo-and-add
plays.how: “Baibai” → “Baibai! Bye-bye, car!” (Wk 3)

plays.name: Family photo book
plays.how: “Where’s yeye?” Let her pat the photo. Echo any name she says. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Quiet board book
plays.how: No buttons. Point and name, wait for her to point back. (Wk 1)

plays.name: Banana or cracker?
plays.how: Hold up two things. Any reach, look or point is her answer: name it. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Three-cup shuffle
plays.how: Hide a toy under one of three cups and move it while she watches. (Wk 3, harder)

plays.name: Stack & crash
plays.how: Stack blocks together; she tries to put one on top, then crashes them. (Wk 1)

plays.name: Lid lab, harder
plays.how: Lids that pull off, then lids that push on; a box with a slot to post things through. (Wk 1, harder)

plays.name: Freeze dance
plays.how: Music on: bounce. Off: “FREEZE!” (Wk 3)

plays.name: Rhythm copy
plays.how: Tap a pot twice, wait, copy what she does. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Gesture songs
plays.how: Itsy Bitsy, Wheels on the Bus. Pause before the gesture so she fills it in. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Copy-me
plays.how: Wipe the table, phone to ear, brush hair. She copies, then you copy her. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Wipe-up helper
plays.how: Damp cloth after meals; she “cleans” her tray. (Wk 1)

plays.name: Solo play + check-ins
plays.how: 4–6 toys out, play together briefly, then “I’ll be right here.” Smile when she looks back. (Wk 3)

plays.name: Peer time side by side
plays.how: 1–2 babies at the playground or a class. No need to share. (Wk 3, good daycare prep)

plays.name: Daytime night-night
plays.how: Lie on her floor bed together, “shhh”… “Good morning!” (Wk 3)

plays.name: Messy tray
plays.how: Yogurt, soft noodles or water on a tray. Squish, pour; you name “sticky, wet, cold.”

plays.name: Water table pouring
plays.how: Cups, a funnel, floating toys. Always within arm’s reach; empty after play.

steps.do: If it keeps flying, lift her out calmly.
steps.say: All done. We’ll eat again later.

scripts.note: Same words every meal. She’s learning, not misbehaving.

steps.do: Smile, pause, wait for her next sound.
No “say it again.” Just enjoy it.

scripts.note: Words grow when they get warm attention, not a test.

steps.say: Mama’s going. Grandma stays. Mama comes back.

steps.do: Leave even if she cries. Come back warm.

scripts.note: Short, same every time. Tears at goodbye are normal and pass.

steps.say: This is our friend. You can watch.

steps.do: Chat warmly with the person so she sees you’re relaxed.

steps.say: You can say hi when you’re ready.

scripts.note: No forced hugs or holding. Her pace.

timeline.hint: Each step can take days or weeks. She may skip around.

steps.label: Standing without noticing
steps.note: Lets go while busy, then sits or grabs back. (now)

steps.label: Noticing she’s standing
steps.note: Stays up on purpose, maybe with a proud look

steps.label: Standing up in the open
steps.note: From a squat, with nothing to hold

steps.label: 1–3 steps
steps.note: Couch to you, falling into your arms

steps.label: Walking more than crawling
steps.note: Feet wide, arms up, lots of falls (normal)

steps.label: Steady walker
steps.note: Carries toys, turns, squats to pick up

ruler.label: When healthy babies first walk alone (WHO):

timeline.footer: Many walk at 12–15 months; 16–18 is still normal. Ask the pediatrician if she isn’t walking alone by ~18 months, or anytime you’re worried.

details.title: Why she won’t say it when asked
lines: Saying a word on her own uses the moment (Baba walks in → “baba!”). Saying it on cue means pulling the word from memory with no trigger. That’s harder and comes later.
Being watched and waited on can also feel like pressure, so she goes quiet.
Understanding comes first, then words on her own, then words on request.

details.title: Why throwing peaks around now
lines: She just learned to let go on purpose. Releasing things is new and fun.
She is studying gravity and that things still exist when they fall (object permanence).
Hunger fades fast at this age. When the tummy is full, food becomes a toy.

details.title: Why calm now, and a new wave soon
lines: Development comes in cycles: a new skill brings a fussy, clingy dip, then a calmer stretch once the skill settles. Exploring on her own has brought her into a calm stretch.

Walking and daycare are the next big changes. Separation protest often peaks somewhere between 9 and 18 months, as she understands you exist when you’re gone but can’t yet predict when you’ll be back.
A consistent goodbye and a warm return teach her the pattern. Most babies settle into daycare within a few weeks.

details.title: Why barefoot is great
lines: Bare feet feel the floor, so balance and foot muscles work better.
Outside or on rough ground: soft, flexible shoes with a wide toe box once she walks.

watch: Won’t bear weight on her legs, or legs seem stiff or floppy
Loses skills: stops babbling, waving, or saying words she had
Uses one side much more than the other
By 12 months: no pointing or waving, doesn’t respond to her name, doesn’t look where you point
By ~16 months: no words in any language (count both)
Fever 100.4°F / 38°C or higher, or a teething baby who seems really sick (teething doesn’t cause high fever)
Seems not to hear. CDC: don’t wait.
